D008-D003_h004.question_both:
I’ve been feeling completely out of control for the past few months. There was this one month where I barely slept—maybe two or three hours a night—but I didn’t feel tired. My mind wouldn’t shut off, ideas racing, jumping from one thing to the next. I’d start projects at school, rearrange faculty schedules, draft new policies, but never finish any of them. I felt wired, pacing my office, snapping at staff when things didn’t move fast enough. One minute I’d feel on top of the world, like I could fix everything; the next, I’d be furious over small things. But then it faded, and I crashed.  

For the next two months, I just shut down. I called out of work, canceled meetings, stopped returning calls—even from my husband. I couldn’t get out of bed most days. There were times I felt like I’d ruined everything: my school, my family, like I was somehow responsible for every bad thing that’s happened lately, even things that aren’t my fault. Like I’ve brought misfortune just by existing.  

It’s hard to tell when it’s stress or something deeper. I’ve always been intense, but this feels different. I don’t know if it’s new or if it’s been this way forever and I’ve just ignored it.
D008-D003_h004.question_a:
I’ve been going through extremes that I can’t control. For the past month, I felt like I was on fire—like I could run the school, the district, maybe even the whole state. I wasn’t sleeping—three hours, sometimes none—and I didn’t care. My mind raced so fast I couldn’t keep up. I’d start five things at once: rewriting policy, renovating my office, planning events—none of it got finished. I snapped at teachers over tiny things, then minutes later felt this bizarre euphoria, like everything was meant to happen. I couldn’t sit still, pacing, talking fast, jumping between ideas.

Before that, though, for about two months, it was the opposite. I barely got out of bed. I stopped calling friends, even my sister. I felt responsible for every bad thing—my students’ failures, a car accident downtown—like I’d caused them. I had no energy, but that’s not the point—the guilt felt real, even though I know it doesn’t make sense. 

The restlessness and not sleeping? That’s only ever like this during these episodes. I wasn’t like this as a kid. This isn’t who I am—it’s like I get taken over.
D008-D003_h004.question_b:
I’ve always been this way, even as a kid—my teachers said I was “driven” or “always on the go,” but it’s just how my brain works. I don’t know what it’s like to sit still or quiet my thoughts. The racing ideas, not being able to finish what I start, the constant need to *do* something—it’s been there since elementary school. I remember bouncing my leg in class, talking over others, and getting in trouble for blurting out answers.  

Lately, though, it’s worse. For the past month, I’ve barely slept—some nights not at all—and I don’t feel tired. I start projects at school, reorganize entire departments, jump into new initiatives, but never finish them. I talk fast, nonstop, and I can feel my mood swinging within minutes—jubilant one moment, snapping at staff the next. But here’s the thing: even when I’m not like this, the restlessness, the mental chatter, the impulsivity—they never go away.  

And then there were those two months last year when I shut down completely—didn’t want to see anyone, felt like I’d ruined my family, my school, even the world, as if disasters were my fault. But the lifelong pattern—that’s not a mood episode. That’s me. Always.
